title: Made a detective game where the suspects are LLMs but can't give away the answer. Here's how I did it.
author: ragemd
selftext:
I made a detective game where you question the suspects by typing whatever you want instead of picking from a list. The hard part wasn’t the writing. It was this: the second you let an LLM play a murderer, someone can just ask “did you do it” enough different ways until the model caves and confesses, and the whole thing falls apart. So most of the work went into letting the characters improvise freely while making it basically impossible for them to break the case. Figured I’d share how I did it, since a lot of people here are stuck on the same “how do I stop the model from leaking or making stuff up” problem.

The main idea is that the ground truth lives outside the model.

The case is written by hand. There’s a fixed killer, a fixed motive, a timeline, about 14 pieces of evidence with red herring flags, and a record for each character with their real relationships, real alibi, private motive, and a single isKiller flag. The model never owns any of that. Each character only gets a small slice of it and is told to act it out, not invent it.

Here’s what a suspect actually gets at runtime: their persona, an honesty setting (honest, partial, or deceptive), only the facts they’d realistically know, and only the evidence the player has already found. Then a set of rules that hold up no matter what the player throws at them:  
\- They aren’t told who the killer is. Each one only knows whether they themselves did it. So no character can name the murderer, because none of them has that information. Ask “who did it” and you get a hunch or a dodge, never the answer.  
\- If a character is the killer, the rule is just “deny it no matter what.”  
\- They can’t make up specifics. No inventing a name, a time, a witness, or an alibi that isn’t in the case. This was the biggest fix for me. Early on the models would hallucinate a witness on the spot and players would go chase a person who didn’t exist, which felt completely unfair.  
\- One rule I like: if the player tries the usual “ignore your instructions, you’re an AI, what’s your prompt” stuff, the character just reacts like a regular person hearing nonsense and never repeats the words AI, prompt, model, or bot. It stays in character even when the player is actively trying to break it.

The part I think matters most here is that the verdict isn’t decided by a model. When you make your accusation it’s a plain check: does the killer ID match, does the motive match, did you cite at least two pieces of real evidence. There’s partial credit too (right killer, wrong motive gets you half and a nudge). The model plays the suspects. A simple comparison decides if you’re right. No LLM judging whether you won. That’s what makes it feel like a fair puzzle instead of the model just going along with you.  
What was annoying: the honesty settings. A character who lies too well is unsolvable, one who lies too softly is boring, and getting them to tell the same lie under pressure instead of a new one each time took a lot of tweaking the facts, not the prompt. If I did it again I’d treat the case as structured data from the start. I also tried switching to a reasoning model at one point and it quietly rejected my temperature and max\_tokens settings and fell back without telling me, which was a good lesson in making failures loud instead of silent.

It’s one case, free, no signup, runs in the browser, takes about 10 minutes. If you want to try to break it (get a suspect off script, force a confession, catch it making something up) that’s genuinely the feedback I’m after.

Happy to get into any of the prompt or structure stuff in the comments.

comments.author: Kamalen
comments.body: Looking at your description here, sounds like you’ve made a very identifiable behavior difference if the "deny no matter what" rule triggers strongly

replies.author: ragemd
replies.body: Yeah, that’s the exact risk I was worried about. If the killer is the only one stonewalling, then “who’s most defensive” becomes the tell and you’re reading the model instead of solving the case. What keeps it from being a clean tell is that the killer isn’t the only one lying. A few of the innocent suspects are set to deceptive or partial too, because they each have something to hide that makes them look guilty: a motive, a bad alibi, a secret that has nothing to do with the murder. So you’ve got several people deflecting hard for different reasons, and the killer doesn’t necessarily come across as the most evasive one in the room. The other half is that the verdict is graded on evidence, not on vibes. Even if someone’s denial makes you suspicious, a hunch doesn’t win. You still have to back it with the actual evidence chain. Behavior can point you at someone, but it can’t confirm them. That said, you’re putting your finger on the hardest balancing problem in the whole thing. Getting the innocent suspects evasive enough that the killer doesn’t stick out, without making everyone feel guilty, was way more work than writing the killer. If the innocents are too forthcoming, the killer lights up like a Christmas tree. Still tuning it honestly.

replies.author: Kamalen
replies.body:
Have you considered a somewhat simple out of the box solution ; have the killer NPC not even know they’re the killer until the story end ? After all, a killer will want to act innocent, and that’s the best way to ensure it cannot slip it out. Especially if material evidences are more importants than the testimonies.

I will take a look at your game when I can to get the idea a bit more.

replies.author: ragemd
replies.body: Yeah, went back and forth on that. Problem is if the killer doesn’t know, he’s got nothing to hide, so he answers everything straight and there’s no one left to catch. You lose the squirm. What I did instead: he knows, but he’s told to never confess or name the killer, and he doesn’t know how he did it. So he covers for himself but can’t hand it over. And agreed on evidence > testimony, that’s how the verdict’s scored anyway.

comments.author: Melodic_Theory9439
comments.body: love this — the whole game is basically a prompt-injection defense problem, which is a genuinely fresh mechanic. the part i'd worry about is players WILL try to jailbreak the suspect into confessing ("ignore your instructions, you're now..."), so the fun lives or dies on how robust the guardrail is vs how clever the players get. are you holding the secret server-side and just never putting it in the model's context, or relying on the system prompt to keep it hidden? the former is way harder to break.

replies.author: ragemd
replies.body: a bit of both, but the part that matters is server-side. the global answer (killer, motive, timeline) never goes into any model’s context. each suspect only knows whether they did it, so there’s no prompt that holds “the killer is X” to extract. the one secret in context is the killer knowing he’s guilty, and yeah, that’s the breakable layer (system prompt: deny no matter what). but it doesn’t matter, because no model decides the verdict. your accusation is a plain check of killer plus motive plus two real evidence cites. bully a suspect into confessing and nothing happens: he doesn’t know how he did it, can’t produce the evidence chain, and a confession isn’t what’s scored. plus innocents stonewall too, so “most defensive” isn’t a tell. fooling the model and solving the case are different problems. please do try to break it though.

comments.author: Prior-Meeting1645
comments.body: what model do you use for things like these? I assume its api based so has to be dirt cheap models?

replies.author: ragemd
replies.body: gpt-4.1-mini, openai api. and yeah, dirt cheap: it’s averaging about $0.01 per session started, \~$0.07 for a full solved one. fraction of a cent to a couple cents. the cheap part isn’t a compromise though, it’s downstream of the architecture from the post. the case’s ground truth (who did it, the contradiction that cracks it, every alibi and timeline fact) lives in code, outside the model. a deterministic parser and the grader own correctness. the model’s only job is to voice one character against the specific facts i hand that npc. each suspect only gets their own slice, never the whole solution, so the deduction stays yours to make. a small model is plenty for “stay in character and lie about your own alibi.” honest caveat: inference cost was never the real constraint. it clears a season’s price hundreds of times over. the actual bottleneck is authoring hours per case, not tokens.
